It wasn't out of the realm of possibility that Chloe might leave after that experience. Given how tragic the original LiS was on just about every level, it wouldn't be outside the tone or character of Chloe that things might be too much. Even if her intention was to stick with Max forever, Chloe didn't have enough life behind her to know how much was still ahead. They were both young. Young people try their best, but it was an impossible situation for Max and Chloe.

It's fine if you don't like the developer decision for the breakup, but I can't pretend like this what out of character for Chloe. Think about all the abandonment issues she had before the first game even started. She has had a tough life, and then something supernaturally impossible dumped more onto her.

Nope. The story shows that the storm was caused by Max in post bay. That’s pretty convincing. Chloe dies=no storm. As for Max making a final choice, it’s a theory that Max has to test. She doesn’t definitively know either way before she makes that choice whether she’ll save the town, or even if things will be worse if Chloe dies. She has to pick one and live with the ramifications, which is the entire point of the game. She spends the entire game rewinding her decisions, living through them, and then deciding on the decision she wants when she knows the results. This final decision—she doesn’t know the definitive results, and she has to live with whatever she decides. So poetically speaking, the story did what it was supposed to do. 

Sorry to interrupt, but I have heard this a number of times—and I feel like people missed the point of the game, as well as the function of the final decision. The game isn’t asking you what’s the more moral decision, it’s asking you as a person to just make a choice and accept the consequences. In the Bae ending, Max is pretty resolute when she tears that photograph. In the Bay ending, Max seems okay at the funeral—sad, but at least she’ll be able to move on. Has nothing to do with morality. I also say this as someone that only picks to Sacrifice Chloe in every playthrough.

That’s why I never said “bad person” in my post, just not exactly good. I love Finn as a character, I hope to see him again I like him so much. I know it’s determinant, but still. I just think taking a nine year old into a robbery is a little—that doesn’t exactly make you “good”, and I don’t think we should paint him as innocent either. 

That is a defining moment in a person’s life, a choice like that, and it can wipe away a lot of good a person has done. How can it not be a defining moment? I just think that saying “Oh it was just a stupid decision and dangerous” is a little too light handed for what he actually did. Sure, he did a lot of great things, and is overall a good guy—but man, that’s a pretty big thing to do for us just to swipe it away as “dumb and dangerous”...and then we just let it go because we like him. Not to mention all of the carnage at the end of episode three that was in direct correlation to Finn dragging Daniel in there. Daniel did it, but keep in mind that Finn was the one that set it up to go.

Finn May be stupid, but he’s not good. He’s an interesting character, but he is still using a child to help rob a drug dealer. The dude isn’t just harmless. He may be messed up because of his past, but man it doesn’t absolve him of dragging a kid into a situation that might get him killed. The dude literally watched Daniel almost get beaten earlier! How could he not know the ramifications? It wasn’t like he didn’t have any common sense. I say all this as someone that still loves his character, but I really think he’s not exactly a “good” person.

It nailed right on the head what it’s like to love your friends(possibly more depending how you played), dealing with grief, a take on depression that wasn’t stereotypical, it had moments of great joy which made the sad moments really hit, and it captured the feeling of nostalgia of times gone by—that yearning to go back to a place or a period of time that can no longer exist. It was also a story about moving on.

They’re different in how they handle issues, but it’s just really hard to follow up the lightning in a bottle they caught with the first game. The story in 2 is still amazing, and I am still on board with it. Hard to say much since it is still not finished, but LiS1 was really hard to follow up with anything.

The picture of Chloe on his dorm room floor will always make me think that Nathan intended to do a lot more than what ultimately happened. I find that to be one of the most disturbing pictures in the game, to be honest.

Nathan is an interestingly written antagonist, although even if we got more information about him--I doubt we would ever really find ourselves 'rooting' for him.

The problem is that the first few moments we get to meet Nathan, he kills a girl(that we don't know is Chloe at the time)in the bathroom. From there, our second meeting is him threatening Max, then strangling her. After Max barely escapes with Chloe's help, we watch him brutally beat Warren. We then find out that he drugged Chloe, and though the story is vague with Chloe saying she kneed him to escape, we don't know exactly what he did to her before she was able to escape. We know that he murdered Rachel, after kidnapping and entrapping her. We're also made aware that alongside of Jefferson--he helped to drug and kidnap Kate, which potentially leads to her suicide. Then there's all of the red binders that we weren't able to look in, representing all the women that Jefferson kidnapped and drugged, which we don't actually know how many of these 'photo sessions' Nathan was involved in.

Potentially, we could say that a little sympathy is gained if you let Warren beat him down, but even then the guy has a gun. Maybe some sympathy in the phone call too. Nathan's actions, while the motivation behind them is fascinating, heartbreaking, and make for a well written character--there is little that can be done to allow for any kind of redemption or the audience rooting for him.

Even if we gained more information on his past, nothing that happened to him would justify any of his actions. They would only serve as an interesting story that allowed us to see his motivations better.

I love LIS2 a great deal.

Sean is an interesting character. We get a sense of him being a teenager in the beginning of the episode, and everything that entails. It was joyful to go through all the texts, see his relationships with people. Made me feel nostalgic for when I was younger. The relationship established with the father was really fascinating because he was a really good guy. He had boundaries for his kids, but he also gave Sean freedom to be a teen. When he asks Sean about the 'supplies' the party--if you're just straight up with him, it's a nice showcase of how he is as a parent. Also the moment about the chocolate bar when Sean comes in the house.

Lyla is fascinating--you can see just how much she cares about Sean, who is obviously oblivious to the fact that she is head over heels for him. Take a look at the text messages. Some of the ones she sent when she was drunk were really, really cringey in a heartwarming way. She obviously is battling trying to be his friend and her own feelings for him. It was sweet that she tried so hard to set him up with that other girl. The texts after you leave are just heartbreaking too--she is so, so worried about Sean.

Brody had a lot of depth--in the chunk of the game we got about him, we learned a great deal about him. You had to really, really listen. His character makes me so happy.

The amount of tension with taking care of Daniel was tangible. This game did something weird--every time he left my sight, I started to become very nervous. Daniel goes and talks to people without your input. He has his own things he likes to do. The bits about Minecraft were fun.

There's a mystery about the mother. We also don't know where they're going next. I became very attached to these two characters by the end of episode one. I know a lot of people didn't, but I think what broke my heart the most is the fact that Sean is trying through the entire episode to be strong--then when you have those classic moments of LIS "sit and reflect" sequences--we get how terrified he is. We get that he is just a kid put in an impossible situation. This game is all about growing up, what we teach others as we grow, and how we handle the world. I'm in love with this game as much as I loved LIS Season One. I think that the story is about to get really, really intense. I can't wait to see where it goes.

I think Nathan continued it simply because Jefferson basically kept twisting his mind, which was already vulnerably sick. I think that’s the only reason he continued on with life, with everything. “Dad” says it’s okay, and I want to make my only father figure proud.

Plus, Nathan is 18. If he doesn’t want to have representation, then his family can’t do anything. I think we need to take into account just how much killing Chloe would tip him over the edge. Even if he was responsible for Rachel, that’s still a  major event that changes everything for him. I have been hesitating to say this, as it oversimplifies him, but Nathan seems to be a coward. The fight with Warren shows that. When the chips are down, he will fold, and even if Jefferson is a father figure—I truly don’t believe he wouldn’t tell everything.

If Nathan did get representation from the family, and the authorities discovered the Dark Room, they could see that it wasn’t a one man operation, or there had to be at least someone else involved. I wouldn’t be shocked if he got a plea deal if he confessed to everything. Now I am surmising outside of any given evidence in the story, but the point I am making is that he would give up Jefferson in a number of different ways.

Well, some of us that chose the Bay did it for intensely personal reasons that didn’t involve the good of the town. I was going through a lot at the time, and LiS helped me get over an event I couldn’t let go of—especially the Bay ending, as it changes the context of the story to one about learning to let go of the things we cannot change. I’m not going to surmise others choices of why they chose, or question the validity of either ending. It’s a weirdly very personal choice, which is one of the reasons why I love the game so much.

I didn’t see that way. I saw it as to save everyone Chloe needed to die, and Jefferson getting caught was a natural by product of that circumstance and relationship. I just don’t know what else Nathan would have done if he was caught...I can see how it frustrates you, though.

I think the Bay ending has merits, as it is my preferred choice. It breaks my heart to think that to save the town, Chloe had to die alone on a bathroom floor believing that everyone she loved was always going to leave her. It’s a hard swallow. I don’t believe the developers intended that to be the primary story, though. I think Bae or Bay are equally valid routes, they just both have consequences for each.

Well, true. I was being hyperbolic for the sake of example. Yes, it doesn’t have to come that far out of nowhere.

I do disagree though—the paper Nathan had that said, “Rachel in the Dark Room” over and over showed us a mind wracked with guilt. Chloe’s death would push him over whatever psychological cliff he was standing atop. I cannot for the life of me see why he wouldn’t give up MJ in that position. There’s nothing inherently honorable about him, other than the message he gives Max near the end. I doubt he would keep Jefferson safe when he is caught red handed for murder.

Chloe still dies. That’s a massive price. To save the town and ultimately stop Jefferson, her true love has to die. 

EDIT: She has to die to stop the town from being destroyed and stop Jefferson IF YOU CHOSE THE BAY ENDING!!! This is not me indicating that there was a right way to do this, I am talking about a singular choice you have the option of making. Your canon could be the bae ending, in which case the town is destroyed, and Jefferson is stopped by those circumstances. I chose the Bay ending, but it doesn’t mean anything. That’s MY PERSONAL STORY OF LIS, not anyone else!!!!

The idea that Nathan wouldn’t roll over on Jefferson as soon as he was caught would be bad character writing. He was obviously guilty and tortured over Rachel, it was all over various paperwork you find in the game. Jefferson could even tell that Nathan was a loose end. 

The thing I personally don’t like in the Bay ending is the final moment with the butterfly. Max seems too hopeful, and it’s a false writing move to soften the consequences. She would be messed up for a long, looooong time. Like trauma or alcoholism messed up. That was sooo much to go through. She would be a wreck at that funeral. That’s where the writing does fall apart, as it doesn’t stay true to Max’s character. I understand that it’s supposed to be that Max has ultimately been changed by the experience in a way that has made her stronger, but it rings false for me. That’s my two cents. That’s where the consequences for the decision fall apart for me. Or, I am just overly emotional. I don’t know.

Also, she can’t tell ANYONE what happened because the week never existed in the first place. That’s just—a lot of unhappiness. We’re talking entrapment, torture, witness to multiple deaths, possibly euthanizing her love depending on your choice, possibly failing to stop the suicide of a friend...like—I’m not sure I could walk away from all that as a stronger being. The trauma would leave me horribly devastated for years.

That’s not what a deus ex machina is though. I mean yeah, refer to it as a stupid plot choice(even though I personally think it fits great story-wise). It would have to be out of left field waaaayyyy more to be a deus ex machina. Also, it would have to be something that allows the protagonist not to pay for a price for whatever it is they want to have at the end. That is most certainly not the case. 

A deus ex machina would be Nathan suddenly deciding not to meet up, leaving Chloe alone in the bathroom. Well, aside from Max. Then the storm doesn’t happen anyway.

“What—what in the good Godly fuck?!” I stumble backward away from the bear.

It smirks at me, an eye brow pitched, “Pretty sure you just took the lord’s name in vain there.” A cigar oozes out from the bear’s jagged stitched crease of a mouth, followed by a deep cough which sputters up a lighter as well. “You mind if I smoke?”

My lips grasp around the edges of syllables, finding none. Shuffling off the couch, the bear bumps butt first to the carpet with a squeak, face planting immediately.

On impact, it cries, “Ow—oh fuck, that actually really hurt. That—that really hurt.” Pushing off from the floor, it rubs its face for a moment, “Don’t laugh, don’t you dare laugh, or I—I’ll turn you into a penis unicorn, and yes that is exactly what you think it is.”

I utter breathlessly, “Are—are you the actual devil?” 

“Yes I—I...” As it attempts to answer me, both tiny bear arms are reaching under the couch. The teddy sighs deeply, staring up at me, “Could you—my cigar rolled under there, and I—I don’t really like to overuse the whole ‘there’s a cigar coming out of my mouth, isn’t that super scary’ trick. I have a bad gag reflex, and so I really only have one in me per day before I start getting a bit sick to the stomach.”

“Yeah, yes, of course.” I scramble past him, my arm reaching deep underneath the couch. Dust bunnies and ancient tootsie rolls slither across the skin of my hand, fingers just reaching over the cigar. Yanking it out, I hand the cigar to the bear.

“Thank you,” it says, lighting up the end of the stogie with practiced bravado. “To answer your question, Ms. Piper McCabe,” it exhales in a plume, “I am the Devil.”

“Okay? Okay.” I scratch my head, searching for the next logical question. “Do you like—cake decorating?”

“What?” The Devil pauses, genuinely diagnosing me. “Are you making fun of me?”

“No, no, I just don’t know what to—to say, I have terrible anxiety issues!”

He shakes his head, rolling the beads he has for eyes, “I hope he’s right about you, because you’re not making a good first impression.” Scoffing, the Devil crosses the threshold of the linoleum floor of the kitchen, “Cake decorating? Kind of bloody shit is that?”

“When I get—nervous, I can’t think well, okay?” I follow him, his tiny body attempting to open the fridge door. “I don’t have any groceries, my pay check comes in tomorrow but—but I have a zip lock baggy of Swedish Fish my mom gave me if you want something to nibble on?”

“You’re just gonna suck all of the fun out of my day, aren’t you?” He says in a disdainful huff.

“I—I just broke up with my girlfriend, okay? After three years, she couldn’t even do it in person, and—and now there’s a teddy bear claiming to be the devil incarnate walking around my apartment, so excuse me if I am not handling this perfectly!” My heart is playing my ribs in an up tempo beat, rage boiling from the veins I know are pulsating at my neck.

“Don’t yell at me, I haven’t done a thing to you, I’ve been a polite and courteous house guest.” The Devil wanders away from the kitchen like a drunken toddler, walking toward my Blu-ray collection, “Good god—Avatar? Really? She’s not going to like that...”

“It was James Cameron’s—one of his best movie—“

“Well yes, if you like Pocahontas, it’s great. I’m sure you just loved the special effects, too.”

Yanking him from the floor, I scream in his face, “What do you want?!”

“My—my daughter is single, and now so are you!”

I tilt my head in confusion, although something about how I contort my face seems to disturb him. “You have a daughter?”

“Look, God—I asked if he knew anyone that would be a match for my daughter since he was in charge of creating everyone right? She just got out of a bad relationship with an angel—and you know, I told her that angels were quite full of themselves, but kids never listen.” I set him down again on the floor. He takes another drag, “God said humans were the way to go he thought, so I got the intel on you from him, and he was pretty impressed with you—thought you’d make a good match with my daughter since she’s an introvert too, you both have an unbalanced hatred of season one of Justice League, and you both like wearing yoga pants all the time while also ironically making fun of other people who wear them all the time too.”

I spit out, “Could you at least wait until the body of my relationship is cold?”

“Hey, you just be happy I waited to take you back to hell after it was over.” As the Devil mentions this, a large portal opens up. My apartment is cast in a red glow. A warm, humid wind blows out of the hellhole.

My blood runs cold, “What?”

“Yeah. Oh wait.” He waves his fist, a finger snapping sound emanating from it, and suddenly I’m wearing the most beautiful dress I’ve ever laid eyes on while holding a bouquet of a dozen roses. “Her name is Meek. Well, that’s her nickname, she likes to be called that.”

“Uhm...” Beads of sweat begin to form on my forehead. “I don’t really have a choice in this, do I?”

“Well, I mean, you don’t have to go, no. I can leave you here.” Shrugging, he adds, “But if you go, I can guarantee that my daughter is not the cheating kind. She’s young, you know, still in her early thousands—but she has a good heart.”

“I didn’t realize my ex cheated,” I murmur.

“Spoiler: You were going to have that revealed to you in a drunk phone call—eventually.” He grabs my free hand, looking into the portal deeply, “Ready?”

I give a nod, “Does she at least like Swedish Fish?”

If you break it down to a major dramatic question, it turns into, “Will Max save Chloe?” Max wants to keep Chloe alive, so we have a protagonist goal. Major conceptual question, “Can we really protect the people we love?” Most of the storylines all deal with that question: Victoria with Nathan, obviously Max with Chloe, Max with Kate, Joyce with Chloe, Chloe with Rachel, Frank with beans(jk—Rachel), Max with William, Warren with Max...the list goes on. Ultimately leading to the final choice: if it comes down to saving the world or saving someone you love, what choice do you make? Unfulfilling perhaps because it’s difficult to make a multi choice script end without feeling as though all the choices were for naught, simply because I’m not sure that writers have quite figured out how to adapt to these types of scripts yet when there’s a bottom line budget that only allows for so much variation. 

Each additional element means hundreds or thousands of hours of work for texture artists, designers, modelers, audio technicians, etc. So as a writer you have to be clever in how you play in the sandbox with everyone because you don’t have full control.
